title: Treaty, Convention and Protocol
canonical_question: Write short notes on Treaty, Convention and Protocol.
present_day_examinable_core: What each of the three words denotes, and - the point the examiner is actually testing - that these titles do not create a legal hierarchy. A distinct examinable task from the PROCESS by which an IMO convention is adopted and enters into force.

recommended_exam_depth.note: MIW's recommendation for one limb of a four-limb 'write short notes on any THREE' question. The sittings that evidence this family print a paper total only, with no per-question or per-limb split.

understand_first: MIW EXPLANATION - secondary to the legal foundation set out in the model answer, and not itself the definition. The trap in this limb is that the three words are not three parallel things, and the trap behind that one is assuming the difference between them is a difference of RANK. It is not. Treaty is the generic category, defined by Article 2(1)(a) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969. Convention and protocol are designations given to instruments, and Article 2(1)(a) applies to an agreement meeting its criteria 'whatever its particular designation' - so an instrument titled Protocol may itself be a treaty, and its title places it above or below nothing. These titles do not create a hierarchy, and neither designation occupies a position on a ladder. The second thing worth seeing is what a protocol actually did in one concrete case. MARPOL is the standing example - the 1973 Convention did not enter into force on its own, and it was after the 1978 Protocol that the combined instrument entered into force on 2 October 1983. That is MARPOL's own history, and it is not a general rule about what protocols do.

blocks.p: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 (VCLT), Article 2(1)(a) defines a treaty as an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law, whether embodied in a single instrument or in two or more related instruments, and whatever its particular designation. That last phrase is the operative one for this limb: the designation of an instrument does not determine whether it falls within that definition. An instrument is a treaty if it meets those criteria, whatever its particular designation.

Read Article 2(1)(a) with VCLT Article 3, which preserves the legal force of international agreements that fall outside the Convention's scope - those concluded with other subjects of international law, or not in written form. Article 2(1)(a) is therefore the definition used for the purposes of the Convention, not an exhaustive statement of every international agreement that can bind.

VCLT Article 11 sets out the MEANS by which the consent of a State to be bound by a treaty may be expressed - signature, exchange of instruments constituting a treaty, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, or by any other means if so agreed. VCLT Article 2(1)(b) is the definition provision for four of those named acts: 'ratification', 'acceptance', 'approval' and 'accession' mean in each case the international act so named whereby a State establishes on the international plane its consent to be bound by a treaty.

Article 11 therefore identifies several possible means of expressing consent to be bound, and ratification is not the only means it lists. This is why no rule of the form 'instruments of type X always require ratification' is safe to state.

blocks.h: Convention - Article 2(1)(a) applies whatever the designation

blocks.p: An instrument titled Convention is a treaty where it meets the Article 2(1)(a) criteria. Article 2(1)(a) applies to an agreement meeting those criteria whatever its particular designation.
The designation Convention does not determine whether it falls within the Article 2(1)(a) definition of a treaty.

blocks.h: Protocol - a treaty where Article 2(1)(a) criteria are met

blocks.p: A protocol that meets the Article 2(1)(a) criteria is itself a treaty. Because Article 2(1)(a) applies whatever the instrument's particular designation, its title alone does not alter that conclusion.

The 1978 MARPOL Protocol is related to the 1973 MARPOL Convention. VCLT Article 11 identifies several possible means of expressing consent to be bound, and ratification is not the only means it lists, so there is no universal rule that a protocol must be ratified. The Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) is the worked maritime example, and it permits three distinct routes: signature without reservation as to ratification, acceptance or approval; signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval followed by that act; or accession.

MARPOL is the worked example. The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships was adopted on 2 November 1973 but had not entered into force on its own. Following the tanker accidents of 1976-77 the 1978 Protocol was adopted, and the combined instrument entered into force on 2 October 1983. The 1997 Protocol later added Annex VI. It is given here as what happened to MARPOL - not as a general rule about what protocols do.

rows: The category defined by VCLT 1969, Article 2(1)(a): an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law, and that definition applies whatever its particular designation.
An instrument titled Convention is a treaty where it meets the Article 2(1)(a) criteria, and Article 2(1)(a) applies whatever its particular designation.

An instrument titled Protocol is a treaty where it meets the Article 2(1)(a) criteria, and the title alone does not alter that conclusion. For the Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) permits three routes to becoming a Party: signature without reservation as to ratification, acceptance or approval; signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval followed by that act; or accession.

blocks.h: The distinction to hold on to

blocks.p: The key legal point is that the titles alone do not determine treaty status. Apply Article 2(1)(a) to decide whether an instrument is a treaty, whatever its particular designation.

MIW GUIDANCE - secondary to the legal foundation above, and not a substitute for it. Open with the CATEGORY point in one sentence: treaty is the generic category under VCLT Article 2(1)(a), and convention and protocol are both treaties, because these titles do not create a hierarchy. Then one short paragraph each, anchored on the two instruments this answer actually reads at source: the Vienna Convention 1969 for the definition, and the 1973 MARPOL Convention with its 1978 Protocol for the convention/protocol pair. If you say anything about ratification, say it about the instrument in front of you - the Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) permits three different routes - and never as a universal rule about protocols.

It is not the four stages of an IMO convention. That is a question about PROCESS - proposal and drafting, adoption, acceptance, entry into force - and MIW answers it separately on a solved paper. The two are commonly confused because both involve the words 'convention' and 'entry into force', but an examiner asking for short notes on three instrument types will not accept a narrative about committee procedure. Read the stem, then decide which of the two you are being asked for.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Treaty is the legal CATEGORY: under VCLT 1969 Article 2(1)(a) an agreement between States in written form and governed by international law is a treaty WHATEVER ITS PARTICULAR DESIGNATION - so the title determines neither status nor rank. Convention and Protocol are therefore not legal tiers, and a Protocol meeting those criteria is itself a treaty. VCLT Article 11 identifies several possible means of expressing consent to be bound - signature, exchange of instruments, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, or any other means if so agreed - so ratification is not the only means it lists. The Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) proves it - signature without reservation, or signature followed by ratification, acceptance or approval, or accession - so ratification is not universally required.
keywords: ratification not the only means listed
critical_numbers: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties - 1969
MARPOL - Convention adopted 2 November 1973, not in force independently
MARPOL - the combined instrument entered into force 2 October 1983
Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL - Article IV(1), three permitted routes to becoming a Party
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 - Article 2(1)(a), the definition of a treaty and the words 'whatever its particular designation', which are what make convention and protocol both treaties and prevent any ranking by title; Article 3, which keeps that a definition for the Convention's purposes rather than an exhaustive one; Article 2(1)(b), which defines ratification, acceptance, approval and accession; and Article 11, which sets out the means by which consent to be bound may be expressed. Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) - the worked maritime example of an instrument for which several of those means are agreed.
quick_revision.major_trap: Asserting a legal HIERARCHY - that a treaty outranks a convention which outranks a protocol, or that a protocol is subordinate because of its title. VCLT Article 2(1)(a) applies 'whatever its particular designation', so the designation does not determine whether an instrument falls within that definition. The second trap is the universal claim that a protocol always requires ratification: the means of expressing consent to be bound are those of VCLT Article 11, which identifies several possible means and does not make ratification the only one, and the Protocol of 1978 relating to MARPOL, Article IV(1) permits three different routes. The third is answering the FOUR STAGES of an IMO convention instead, which is a process question MIW answers elsewhere.

authority_sources.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 - Article 2(1)(a), the definition of a treaty
authority_sources.checked: Read at source and confirmed in force and unamended as at 24 August 2026. authority_sources.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 - Article 2(1)(b) (the definitions of ratification, acceptance, approval and accession), Article 3 (agreements outside the Convention's scope retain their legal force) and Article 11 (the means by which consent to be bound may be expressed)
authority_sources.checked: Read at source as part of the definition correction of 26 August 2026. Article 2(1)(b) is a DEFINITION provision - it says what the four named international acts are - and Article 11 is the provision that sets out the MEANS by which consent to be bound may be expressed, including signature and 'any other means if so agreed'. The two are cited separately here because the superseded version 1.0 text collapsed them, listing ratification/acceptance/approval/accession as though they were the only routes. Article 3 is cited so that Article 2(1)(a) is not presented as an exhaustive definition of every international agreement.

authority_sources.source: Protocol of 1978 relating to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973 - Article IV(1), the routes by which a State may become a Party
authority_sources.checked: Read at source as part of the definition correction of 26 August 2026, and used as the worked maritime example that what is agreed for a particular instrument - not its title - determines how consent to be bound may be expressed. Article IV(1) offers three routes: signature without reservation as to ratification, acceptance or approval; signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval followed by that act; or accession. This single provision is what disproves the universal claim, removed at version 2.0, that a protocol always requires ratification.

review_record.notes: Three checks, and the first is the one that justifies this entry existing rather than reusing a solved paper. QP2308-Q7 is the nearest thing in the corpus and it was read in full before this was written. It answers 'list and explain the four main stages of an IMO convention, and the delay between adoption and entry into force' - a PROCESS question - and it is a good answer to that question. It does not distinguish treaty from convention from protocol, which is what this limb asks for; the word 'protocol' appears in it only inside a worked example of the entry-into-force delay. Accepting it as this limb's owner would have been the same FAIL_SCOPE that tranche 002 refused when it declined to let QP2406-Q8 own the Lloyd's Open Form limb, and it would have been slightly worse, because QP2308-Q7 carries NO canonical QI family at all, so the reuse would have routed a candidate to a question the readiness layer knows nothing about. SECOND, the temporal check. Every example used is a completed treaty event and none of them can move, which is stated in the authority note rather than left as an assumption - this is a limb whose content is unusually stable and the record says why, instead of claiming a currency check it did not do. THIRD, the codes paragraph was checked for over-claim: it says a code binds THROUGH the convention that makes it mandatory and names SOLAS chapter IX for the ISM Code, which is correct and is the narrowest form of the point.
